edition.accessCaveat: The user-provided PDF is too large for web-page fetch and failed independent download; full-volume 1889 printed-text witness inspected through transcription at Scribd, with line-level ranges recorded for Dujardin and selected Alphonsus passages; facsimile images not independently reviewed.

fullBodyTextWitness.verification: Twenty-two meditation paragraphs and selected St Alphonsus argument passages examined against transcription in printed 1889 pagination; primary linked PDF oversized and not page-image cross-checked.

editorialOwnership.dujardin: Only editorial preface meditation §III is Dujardin. It is NOT written by St Alphonsus.
editorialOwnership.alphonsus: The Sacrifice of Jesus Christ, Short Explanation, major practical/ascetical treatises originate with St Alphonsus; verify Grimm additions and later contributors individually.
editorialOwnership.anonymousFrenchAuthor: St Alphonsus expressly acknowledges adapting a learned French author's work; Grimm speculates on Pierre de Condren/derivative published by Quesnel but does NOT conclusively identify original.
editorialOwnership.sourceDistinction: Dujardin's Passion/Salvation-allegory is a voluntary meditation; Alphonsus biblical sacrifice is a theological synthesis; Fortescue is a historical-liturgical external check.

publicationConstraints: An original Mass ceremony is not necessarily instituted to dramatize a Bible event; no ritual-history causal claim from Dujardin's analogies.
The Eucharistic Sacrifice makes present the once-for-all offering of Christ sacramentally; do not claim that it repeats all of Scripture or literally re-performs all biblical events.
'Full Bible' means a curated Scripture-horizon reaching from Genesis through Revelation, not a forced link for every biblical book or verse.
Dujardin's dates (e.g. 4000 years) are meditation rhetoric not defensible scientific timeline.
Dujardin's descent to Limbo/Purgatory and remarks about Jesus not being on altar after Communion require Catholic doctrinal and 1962 rubric review before any presentation.
St Alphonsus's eighteenth-century rubrical notes and Grimm's nineteenth-century annotations may not describe 1962 practice.
Edition-aware Latin Vulgate/English Douay/French Crampon links and canonical 1962 prayer IDs required before publish.
Reproduce no full copyright-encumbered modern text; original-source links and attribution maintained; no external navigation substituting for existing Scripture reader.

alphonsusPassageClaims.paraphrase: Typology of scapegoat and Christ bearing sins outside the camp; first is sacrificial foreshadowing, not the historical origin of a named Roman gesture.
Old sacrificial categories superseded in the obedience of Christ; the author quotes Hebrews 10 directly.

Five sacrificial conditions listed by Alphonsus: sanctification, offering, immolation, consumption, participation; schema is the author's theological classification, not a law-text quotation naming all five.
Noah's sweet-smelling holocaust and the Paschal Lamb are named for the sacrificial framework.
The author treats the Incarnation as consecration of Christ the victim, with direct biblical citations of Jesus as sanctified by the Father and the Annunciation.
Christ's once-for-all self-offering; distinguishes the Incarnation as commencement of an offering from its sacrificial fulfilment.

Alphonsus applies the 1290 days without the continual sacrifice to a future suspension of the Mass; this is an **historical interpretive claim under theological/eschatological review**, not a literal 1962 Mass passage or a chronology for the Atlas.
Christ's eternal priesthood according to Melchizedek; author draws on Davidic psalm and Christ's prayer for glorification.

Anonymous French source (as narrated by Alphonsus) interprets glorification at Resurrection as consumption and communion of sacrifice as beatific participation; **not** Alphonsus's preferred conclusion.
Alphonsus explicitly prefers fulfilment of sacrificial consumption and Communion in the Eucharistic Sacrifice, quoting Trent XXII; distinction from anonymous French source must be preserved.
Alphonsus divides exposition into six parts including Canon+Pater noster; this is his explanatory structure, not a certified historical classification or present 1962 card count.
The angelic wording grounds the Gloria; the Collect reflects a feast/day, an important tie to source-owned Propers.
Gospel procession from one side to the other is allegorically linked by author to Jews and Gentiles; not an objective causal history of movement or general claim about Jews.
Offerings before consecration are discussed anticipatorily; do not suggest that ordinary bread and wine are already consecrated by saying Suscipe sancte Pater.
Water and wine as humanity/divinity and Christian communion; expressly distinguishes ecclesiastical precept from divine institution and quotes Trent XXII ch.7.

Cardinal Bona and an anonymous French source provide historical explanations for evolving Offertory prayers; Alphonsus identifies In spiritu humilitatis and the Lavabo text; dates and underlying sources unverified.
Hanc igitur hand extension interpreted through laying hands on victim; page itself does not cite Lev 1:4 chapter and verse.
Alphonsus names the three biblical sacrifices and gives a Christological typology; he also contrasts Innocent III and Aquinas on post-consecration signs of Cross.

Supplices angel: French predecessor favours identifying Christ as Angel of Great Counsel; Alphonsus prefers Thomas's explanation of angelic presentation of church prayers. Do not falsely portray angel lifting physical hosts.
Our Father understood through seven petitions and filial adoption; 1 John 3:1 directly cited, Romans 8:15 mentioned in commentary.
After-Communion thanksgiving Quid retribuam and Calicem salutaris draw on Psalm 115 and Romans 8:32, adding biblical source to a fixed post-Communion prayer.
Last Gospel is John 1; reported claim that Pius V made it universal should be historically checked (earlier late-medieval usages attest the text).

highPriorityHolds.issue: Dujardin DJ20 says 'Jesus is no longer on the altar' after Communion; this cannot imply that Christ is absent from a tabernacle or other consecrated hosts. Quote only in full historical context with doctrinal annotation.

Dujardin DJ16 describes Christ's descent to Limbo and Purgatory; do not imply unqualified doctrine that Christ delivered the souls in Purgatory. Review Catholic dogmatic distinctions concerning limbus patrum before using.
Dujardin DJ03 gives the 'four thousand years' chronology; meditation time idiom, not verified biblical dating.

Dujardin DJ15 uses elevations as a depiction of the crucifixion and separate species as representing Christ's death. Safeguard: the Sacrifice is made present sacramentally and not repeated as new bloody crucifixion.
Alphonsus ALPX07 reads Daniel 12:11's 1,290 days as a future suspension of Holy Mass. Not accepted as a verifiable literal apocalyptic timeline; no map/calendar dating.

Alphonsus ALPX13 characterizes altar-side movements as Jewish rejection and Gentile acceptance. Attribute historical symbolic interpretation; don't turn into a negative generalization about Jewish people or the origins of the gesture.
Alphonsus ALPX09 reports the anonymous predecessor's view then offers his own different conclusion. Split author identity and quote attribution.
Alphonsus ALPX19 compares competing views of the Angel in Supplices; do not present one source's angelic physical transport claim as doctrinal or historical fact.
Full linked PDF could not be downloaded and page screenshot in browsing environment; text witnesses are independently transcribed 1889 pages, not image-facsimile certified.
